label: Entanglement in rotating machinery
summary: Spinning shafts, chucks, augers, belts and pulleys catch a sleeve, glove, bootlace, drawstring or hair and wind it in, dragging a limb or the whole body after it. A tractor PTO shaft at 540 rpm turns 9 times a second, so the wrap starts before anyone can react, and pulling back only tightens it. A 2001 Canadian fact sheet put farm machinery entanglement deaths alone at about ten a year.
signs: PTO shafts, U-joints and couplings between tractors and implements, above all where the master shield or shaft guard is missing, bent or stuck to the shaft
Augers, post-hole diggers, grain elevators and grain mixers run from a parked tractor: stationary jobs like these were half of all PTO entanglements in the most comprehensive study to date
Pins and bolt heads sticking out of a spinning shaft: they snag cloth
Drill presses, lathes and bench grinders, and any exposed belt, pulley, chain or gear where two parts run together
Snow blower augers and discharge chutes jammed with wet snow
Cold, windy days: bulky coats, scarves and wide coverall legs, and gusts that blow loose cloth into moving parts
do: Shut off the engine or power, take the key, and wait until everything has stopped before you clear, adjust, oil or measure anything
Clear a snow blower jam with a long stick, and only with the engine stopped
Walk around a turning shaft, never over it
Wear close-fitting clothes: sleeves rolled above the elbow, laces tucked in, drawstrings removed, long hair tied up and covered; take off rings, watches, chains and scarves
Keep every guard and shield on. With the tractor off, spin a PTO shaft guard by hand: if it turns with the shaft, it guards nothing
On a drill press, clamp the work or hold it in a drill vise so it can't spin; take the chuck key out as soon as the chuck is tight
Before anyone starts a machine, say so out loud, check the others heard, and have them say it back
dont: Don't wear gloves at a drill press, lathe or milling machine: a caught glove pulls the hand in. Around a PTO or auger in the cold, snug leather or insulated gloves catch less than loose mitts, but any glove can still be pulled in, so keep your hands clear
Don't clear a jam or plug with the machine running, even with a stick: you can't let go fast enough
Don't reach through moving pulleys or belts to put a belt back on
Don't run a machine with a shield missing, or step onto a drawbar or across a shaft while the PTO is engaged
ppe: Close-fitting clothing with no loose ends, and long hair tied up and covered, are the real protection
No gloves at drill presses and lathes, where a caught glove pulls the hand in
CSA-certified eye protection at a drill press, against flying chips
firstAid: Stop the machine first: engine off, key out, and block the implement so it can't shift. Never use engine power to turn the shaft: turning it backward by hand may free them, a two-piece shaft may pull apart, and a one-piece shaft may have to be cut or taken apart at an end

Disengaging a PTO can cause extra movement and injury. Cut clothing away only if they need to breathe easier, and keep them as still as you can: movement can worsen spine and internal injuries, cause severe bleeding or let a severed limb fall free

Press hard on bleeding wounds. If pressure fails on an arm or leg, put a tourniquet 5–10 cm (2–4 in) above the wound and at least 2.5 cm (1 in) above any joint, tighten until the bleeding stops and note the time
Severed part: wrap it in a clean damp cloth, seal it in a plastic bag and keep that bag in ice water, not on bare ice or loose in water; keep it with the person
Expect head, spine and internal injuries: keep them still, watch for shock (cool clammy skin, confusion, fast breathing) and get medical help
